lesson.title: The Transcription Machine: RNA Polymerase
lesson.summary: RNA polymerase is the enzyme that synthesizes RNA from a DNA template during transcription, and unlike DNA polymerase, it can begin building a new strand without a primer.
lesson.body:
Just as DNA polymerase is the enzyme responsible for building new DNA strands during replication, RNA polymerase is the enzyme responsible for building new RNA strands during transcription. Like any enzyme, it works by lowering the energy barrier for a specific reaction, in this case the formation of the phosphodiester bonds that link ribonucleotides together into a growing RNA chain. RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand in the 3' to 5' direction and synthesizes the new RNA strand in the 5' to 3' direction, following the same directional convention introduced with DNA polymerase in the earlier chapter on that enzyme.

There is one crucial difference between the two enzymes worth highlighting. DNA polymerase, as described earlier in this unit, cannot start a new strand on its own. It absolutely requires a primer with a free 3'-OH end to extend. RNA polymerase has no such requirement: it can initiate synthesis of a new RNA strand entirely from scratch, without any primer at all. This ability to self-start is part of what allows transcription to begin at a precise location every time a gene needs to be read.

Before it can begin synthesizing anything, RNA polymerase first has to find the correct starting point among the enormous length of DNA in a cell. It does this with the help of other proteins that recognize a specific DNA sequence called a promoter, positioned just before the gene (the subject of the next chapter). Once correctly positioned, RNA polymerase unwinds a short stretch of the double helix to expose the template strand and begins building RNA complementary to it. As the enzyme moves along the gene, it continues to unwind the double helix just ahead of itself while the DNA re-forms its double helix structure behind it, and the newly made RNA strand peels away from the template as synthesis proceeds.

RNA polymerase does have some ability to correct its own errors, but it is generally less strict about accuracy than DNA polymerase. This makes biological sense: an error in an RNA transcript affects only that one temporary copy, which will eventually be degraded and replaced, whereas an uncorrected error in DNA replication becomes a permanent mutation carried forward into every future generation of cells. Eukaryotic cells actually contain more than one type of RNA polymerase, each dedicated to transcribing different categories of genes, with RNA polymerase II being the one responsible for transcribing the protein-coding genes that become messenger RNA.
